newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks say they rushing on Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks say they rushing on Holocaust fund.

text.p: Swiss banks said on Thursday they were already working fast to set up a Holocaust memorial fund and urged New York politicians to study the facts before deciding on a threatened boycott.

Bank spokesmen said they took the boycott threat seriously but were puzzled the New York proposals were made now after Swiss businesses and the government last week agreed to a humanitarian fund for victims of Nazi persecution.

New York city and state warned on Wednesday they might bar government deposits with the banks or make it hard for them to do business in one of the world's top financial centres unless Switzerland compensates Holocaust survivors.

The moves marked the first entry by U.S. state and local governments into a controversy over whether Swiss banks kept millions of dollars deposited in secret acccounts by Jews before and during World War Two.
"This is hard to understand if you look exactly at what has been done already," Swiss Bankers Association spokeswoman Silvia Matile told Reuters.

Matile said the banks were already working at speed with the Swiss government, other business sectors and Jewish groups to complete plans for a Holocaust fund, which was agreed in principle last week under pressure from world Jewish groups.
"I don't believe it was necessary to create extra pressure because the pace is already very fast...and the concept for the fund will be worked out in the coming weeks," she added.

In Geneva, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told a news conference on Thursday he viewed Switzerland's dispute with Jewish groups over the funds as a "public relations disaster" and urged a quick end to the row.
He was responding to a question on whether he thought Switzerland's perceived neutrality as host to the U.N.'s European headquarters had been compromised by the controversy.
Swiss Bank Corp SBC, one of Switzerland's Big Three global banks, said it took the boycott proposal seriously because it could prompt a wider wave of boycott-type steps.

"We are confident that when New York politicians look at what we have done so far they will see that we are working very concretely right now on the kind of thing they are demanding (a fund)," SBC spokesman Michael Willi said.

Since 1995, the banks have moved under Jewish pressure to open a central office for claims to accounts left by Holocaust victims and set up a joint commission with the World Jewish Congress and Jewish Agency to hunt independently through bank records.

The fund is the latest step, although no amount of money has been fixed yet. Talks now between the parties are focused on who should control the purse-strings, which Nazi victims besides Jews should get the money and how much each Swiss sector should pay.
"The talks are advanced. There is clearly a sense of urgency but at the same time things cannot be rushed too much," said one bank source who declined to be named.

Other bank sources said a final blueprint could be made public by the end of February, with the private sector likely to pay in first and the government following later this year due to the added complications of getting parliamentary approval.
Credit Suisse Group said it could not immediately confirm New York City's statement it had $225 million in cash in short-term investments at subsidiary CS First Boston.

But all three banks are vulnerable to adverse publicity in the United States because North America is both a growth market for their lucrative asset management businesses and a base of some of the world's biggest institutional investors.
